title: Normalisation up to third normal form and when to denormalise

videos.script: Last lesson ended with a procedure. Name the things, one table each, ask several in both directions. It works, and it is a habit rather than a rule — which means that when two people disagree about a design, neither of them can say who is right. {{procedure}} Normalisation is the same advice with a proof attached. It has three steps, each one removes a specific kind of repetition, and at the end of the third you can say something a habit cannot: there is no redundancy of this kind left, and here is why. {{three}} Almost everybody teaches it the same way, with the same textbook definitions about partial and transitive dependencies, and almost everybody comes away able to recite them and unable to use them. So we are going to do it the other way round. {{backwards}} We take one badly shaped table, and at each step we ask the only question that matters: what can go wrong here that could not go wrong if it were split? The forms are what the answers turn out to be. {{question}} And then, because this is the half that gets left out, we do the opposite. There are good reasons to deliberately break third normal form — and there is a test for whether yours is one of them, which is the word measured. {{denormalise}}
